Remnants of 93W, now a slowly-rotating trough axis, is expected to
continue bringing scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms
overnight. Then, gradual improvement is expected through Wednesday 
night as light diffusive southerlies ensue thereafter. As Typhoon 
Dolphin (12W) continues to strengthen and pass well northeast of the 
region, this will induce a much stronger monsoonal flow across the 
Marianas, likely to bring another period of elevated showers and much
stronger winds by next week.

Marine...
Combined seas of 3 to 5 feet are expected to decrease through
Thursday night, followed by the arrival of an easterly swell 
generated by distant Typhoon Dolphin and lingering south- 
southwesterly swells. By the weekend, a consistent monsoonal regime 
will ensue, potentially introducing sea conditions hazardous to small
craft.

Tropical Systems...
Typhoon Dolphin is seen to the N of the Marshall Islands, well SE of
Wake Island, centered near 13.3N 171.7E. Dolphin is moving W at 10 
mph. Maximum sustained winds are now 85 mph, with tropical storm 
force winds extending up to 80 miles from the center. Dolphin is 
expected to make a turn toward the WNW, then NW over the next few 
days as it continues to strengthen. Latest guidance shows Dolphin 
could go through rapid intensification, possibly becoming a super 
typhoon Thursday night or Friday. Dolphin is not expected to directly
impact Micronesia or the Marianas, though it is eventually expected 
to move through somewhere between the far northern CNMI and Wake 
Island. Residents of Wake Island need to monitor the progression of 
Dolphin, as it is expected to strengthen into a significant typhoon 
over the next couple of days as it passes S of Wake Island. If 
Dolphin makes a more NW turn toward Wake Island than expected, it 
could become a very dangerous situation for the island. 

For more information on TS Dolphin, please refer to bulletins by the
Joint Typhoon Warning Center under WMO header WTPN31 PGTW and by the
National Weather Service under WMO header WTPQ31 PGUM.

Eastern Micronesia...
The main feature affecting eastern Micronesia continues to be the
monsoon trough. Westerly winds are seen across the region, with
increased moisture and convergence south of the monsoon trough
creating areas of scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms,
mainly near Pohnpei and Kosrae. Convection does look to increase 
over the next few hours at all three locations as the monsoon flow
strengthens south of TS Dolphin. With Dolphin likely to go through 
some rapid intensification some time over the next couple of days, 
this is expected to increase the monsoon flow over eastern 
Micronesia, resulting in more convection across the region. An
overall very unsettled pattern is expected through the end of the
week at Pohnpei and Kosrae, and through the weekend at Majuro.
Although seas will not be too impressive, they could still be choppy
at Pohnpei and Majuro due to moderate to fresh winds producing wind
waves of 4 feet. 

Western Micronesia...
An unsettled monsoon pattern persists across much of Micronesia. The
western portion of the monsoon trough remains anchored just north of
Palau and Yap, with a broad area of convergent, moderate westerlies 
to southwesterlies producing scattered showers across the islands,
and numerous showers just farther east across much of central Yap 
State. Surface observations at Palau showed wind gusts up to 25 kts,
associated with some of the heavier passing showers. Far to the east,
showers are patchy across Chuuk State, but satellite and model trends
point to increasing showers near Weno this evening, and especially 
late overnight as convergence builds across the area. The western
half of the monsoon trough will be semi-stationary north of Yap and 
Palau through the next few days, while the eastern half gradually 
shifts north, with the expected northwest movement of Typhoon
Dolphin. This will take the convergence and showers farther north of
Chuuk, leading to drier conditions there this weekend and early next
week. Meanwhile, at least scattered showers will continue at Palau 
and Yap throughout the week, becoming locally heavy at times, and 
shower coverage will shift slightly farther north over Yap Proper 
late in the week.

Benign marine conditions continue, but seas will become increasingly
choppy late in the week for Chuuk as the west to southwest monsoon
swell builds, wind waves increase, and a long-period swell arrives 
from the northeast, emanating from TY Dolphin. This could bring 
challenges to small craft through the weekend, as well as increasing 
surf along west, north, and east-facing reefs. The magnitude of these
impacts are uncertain, and will depend in part on the movement and 
development of Dolphin far to the northeast. In the meantime,
altimetry and Yap buoy data show combined seas between 2 and 4 feet
near Yap and Palau, and between 3 and 5 feet near Chuuk.
